title: India Summoned Iran's Envoy Over the Killing of an Indian Sailor in the Hormuz Strait. The Death Toll Is Still Rising.
excerpt: New Delhi lodged a formal protest after Iranian missiles killed one Indian and wounded ten more on two UAE tankers. Another Indian is still missing from a separate attack.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India protested to Iran after an Indian sailor was killed in missile strikes on UAE tankers.
  • Ten Indian seafarers were injured, with two seriously wounded in the attacks.
  • At least two Indians have been killed or gone missing in Hormuz attacks within three days.
  • The U.S. and Iran are escalating military tensions over control of the Strait of Hormuz.
  • Nine million Indians work in Gulf states, relying on safe passage through the strait.
India summoned Iran's deputy ambassador on Tuesday and lodged a formal protest over the killing of an Indian seafarer in the Strait of Hormuz, the Ministry of External Affairs said, marking New Delhi's sharpest diplomatic rebuke of Tehran since the Gulf conflict began in February. The protest came after Iranian cruise missiles struck two UAE-flagged oil tankers — the MT Mombasa and the MT Al Bahiyah — as they transited the southern lane of the strait through Omani territorial waters on Monday. One Indian crew member aboard the Mombasa was killed. Ten other Indian seafarers were wounded, two of them seriously, the ministry said. A total of 30 Indians were among the 46 crew members serving on both vessels. "India is deeply concerned by the attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz," the ministry said in a statement. "The targeting of commercial shipping and civilian infrastructure in the region must cease." ## A Week of Rising Danger for Indian Sailors The diplomatic action followed a cascade of attacks on shipping in the strait that have put Indian maritime workers directly in harm's way. On Sunday, an Iranian strike hit the Cyprus-flagged container ship GFS Galaxy after it allegedly attempted to transit an unapproved route. Of the 24 crew members aboard, 11 were Indian nationals. While 23 were rescued by the Omani Navy, one Indian crew member — identified as a third engineer — remains missing. A search operation is underway. > **""India is deeply concerned by the attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz," the ministry said in a statement."** India has now confirmed that at least two Indian nationals have been killed or gone missing in separate attacks in the strait within the span of three days. Another six Indians and two Ukrainians were among those wounded in the tanker strikes. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it targeted the tankers because they had turned off their navigation systems and ignored repeated warnings, but the UAE has condemned the strikes as a "blatant attack" in breach of international law. ## The Broader Crisis The escalation comes as the United States and Iran are locked in an intensifying military confrontation over control of the world's most critical oil chokepoint. U.S. forces have struck Iran for three consecutive nights. President Donald Trump has reinstated a naval blockade on Iranian shipping and proposed charging a 20 percent toll on all cargo transiting the strait — a proposal the United Nations shipping agency immediately rejected as having no legal basis. ![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg) Iran, which declared the strait "closed until further notice" over the weekend, has rejected any arrangement that undermines its control of the waterway. Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi wrote on X that Tehran was the guardian of the strait and would remain so "forever." The hostilities have sent oil prices surging nearly 4 percent to $87 a barrel, with Brent crude at its highest in four weeks. The Indian rupee slumped to 96.20 per dollar — its weakest in over a month — as markets priced in the impact of higher energy costs on Asia's third-largest oil importer.

## What It Means for Nine Million Indians in the Gulf India has roughly nine million nationals living and working across the Gulf states, from construction labourers and domestic workers to engineers and shipping crew. The Strait of Hormuz is effectively a lifeline — not just for oil imports, but for the hundreds of thousands of Indian seafarers and maritime workers who transit the waterway every year. The summoning of Iran's envoy is significant because India has maintained a carefully balanced posture since the conflict erupted in late February, avoiding direct confrontation with Tehran while quietly preparing for disruptions. It has expanded strategic petroleum reserves, negotiated alternative oil supply routes, and launched a special deposit scheme for overseas Indians that has already attracted $10 billion to shore up the rupee.

But with Indian lives now directly at stake in the strait — and the toll on Indian seafarers mounting by the day — New Delhi's patience appears to be thinning. The statement's blunt demand that attacks on commercial shipping "must cease" signals a harder line, even as India continues to host Iranian officials at BRICS ministerial meetings in the same week. For the thousands of Indian families with members working on merchant vessels in the Gulf, the diplomatic protest offers cold comfort. The real question is whether any government can secure the strait long enough for commercial shipping — and the people who crew those ships — to move through safely.
